newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China troops in Hong Kong professional - UK General.
newsitem.headline: China troops in Hong Kong professional - UK General.

text.p: The last commander of British Forces in Hong Kong said on Saturday that relations with an advance guard of Chinese troops sent to the colony were cordial.
Major General Bryan Dutton said the advance party of People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops had lived up to their promise to keep a low profile ahead of the handover to China.
The final British soldier will march out of Hong Kong in 30 days when more than 150 years of colonial rule draws to a close at midnight on June 30.
"The advance party that are here at the moment are honouring the agreement we had with them," Dutton said.
"They are behaving sensibly and we have a practical working relationship. There is good liaison with them," Dutton told reporters.

Many people in Hong Kong were horrified with the PLA's ruthless putdown of the student-led pro-democracy movement around Tiananmen Square in June 1989 and had regarded their arrival in the territory with trepidation.
Dutton, the first commander of British Forces to visit China since the Communist Revolution of 1949, said the PLA sought to create a good impression in Hong Kong.

"There is a desire for them to use Hong Kong as a window on the world to sell the PLA as a modern and effective force," he said after presiding over the disbandment parade of a logistics regiment ahead of the handover.
"I think that the only approach, the only sensible approach, is to take that at face value and to believe that that is their firm intention at this stage."

He said Hong Kong could only wait and see. "It's like any other good resolution," he added. "We will have to see whether the proof of the pudding is in the eating in one month's time, in three months' time and in three years' time."

London agreed to allow a vanguard of PLA troops into Hong Kong to prepare the way for the Chinese garrison, which will take over external defence duties from the departing Britons, so long as they were unarmed and did not wear their uniforms in public when off duty.
A third group of 90 troops drove across the border on Friday to join 106 colleagues already stationed in Hong Kong.
